title: A $10 Chip That Could Put a Lab on Your Wrist
summary:
A spectrometer is a tool that studies light to learn what things are made of. Labs use big, costly ones to test medicines, foods and chemicals. Now, researchers at the University of Cambridge have built one for about $10. It is only a few centimeters wide — small enough, one day, to fit in a health gadget worn on the wrist.

The team calls it a convolutional spectrometer. It works on the light directly, then uses quick math to work out the spectrum. In tests, it correctly named plastics, medicines, coffee, flour and tea every single time. It also measured health markers such as blood sugar without needles, and it kept working from very cold to very hot.

The researchers warn that much more testing is needed before it can become a real medical product. Still, it could lead to cheap, exact sensors for health monitors and food testing.
why_it_matters: One day, a gadget on your wrist might check things like your blood sugar without needles and help make sure the food you eat is safe.
